piezas.titulo: Validation of the comprehensive ICF Core Set for burn injury rehabilitation from the perspective of occupational therapists and patients.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Purpose This study aimed to validate the ICF-CS for burn injury rehabilitation from the perspective of occupational therapists (OTs) and patients. Methods A two-round Delphi study was held with experienced OTs specializing in burn rehabilitation who were also familiar with the ICF framework. These experts contributed through a hybrid panel. Codes were retained if they achieved a consensus threshold of ≥75%. Patient perspectives were collected through semi-structured individual interviews, and their suggestions were subsequently linked to ICF codes. Results Fourteen OTs and nineteen patients participated in this study. Of the 68 original codes, more than 80% reached consensus endorsement. Based on experts' input, 17 new codes were incorporated into the ICF-CS: one in the body functions, ten in the activities and participation (AP), and six in the environmental factors. Additionally, eight new codes were derived from patient input-four related to AP and four linked to environmental factors-which overlapped with experts' suggestions. Conclusion The ICF-CS for burn injury rehabilitation received strong endorsement from OTs and patients. The greater emphasis on the AP domain reflects the central role of occupational therapy in healthcare. Furthermore, environmental factors-shaped by national policies and sociocultural contexts-require greater attention in localized adaptations.

piezas.titulo: Voluntary physical activity and pharmacological treatment with the Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 alleviate regional alterations in cerebral synaptic density and improve behavioral recovery after unilateral labyrinthectomy in the rat
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundUnilateral peripheral vestibular loss induces adaptive mechanisms of cerebral plasticity. The quantified Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761® has been shown to enhance neural plasticity, and is used in the treatment of vertigo and dizziness. We here aimed to investigate, how voluntary physical training in a running wheel (RWT) and oral treatment with EGb 761® affect behavioral recovery and whole-brain synaptic density following chemical unilateral labyrinthectomy (cUL) in the rat.MethodsThirty-two Sprague Dawley rats were divided into 4 groups with different treatment regimens (group 1: control food; group 2: control food + RWT; group 3: EGb 761® food (75mg/day/kg body weight); group 4: EGb 761® food + RWT). All rats underwent a left-sided cUL by transtympanic injection of bupivacaine and p-arsanilic acid. Behavioral testing (scoring of nystagmus, postural asymmetry, head tilt, locomotion tracking in open field) was done weekly until 9 weeks (d63) after cUL. Serial [18F]UCB-H μPET imaging of synaptic density (targeting synaptic vesicular protein 2A) was performed before and up to 9 weeks post cUL. Images were whole-brain normalized and segmented based on Schiffer's atlas. Voxel-wise and regional changes of cerebral [18F]UCB-H uptake were compared across groups and time points.ResultsAll rats showed signs of acute vestibular syndrome following cUL. The EGb 761® + RWT group had a significantly faster and more complete improvement of postural asymmetry by week 5 post UL and a higher locomotor velocity thereafter than the control food group. Compared to baseline, at d63 post cUL the EGb 761® group showed the smalles reduction of synaptic density in the vestibular nuclei of−7.59 ± 7.0 % (vs.−20.37 ± 5.18% in control food group, p < 0.001). In contrast, at d63 post cUL the motor cortex displayed the highest relative gain of synaptic density in the control food group (6.6 ± 3.13 % vs. 0.19 ± 2.81% in the EGb 761® group, p < 0.001). All treatment groups showed an increase of synaptic density in the hippocampal area and the somatosensory cortex at weeks 1-3 post cUL compared to the control food group. The additive effect of EGb 761® and RWT was statistically confirmed in behavior and PET measurements.ConclusionsUnilateral labyrinthectomy induces loss of synaptic density in vestibulo-cerebellar networks, which can be partially reversed by EGb 761® treatment. Combined physical and EGb 761® treatment improves behavioral recovery from cUL most effectively, reinforcing the importance of multimodal treatment in acute vestibulopathies.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de pérdida vestibular: el ejercicio y el extracto de Ginkgo cambian la recuperación. En ratas con laberinto unilateral, el grupo con EGb 761 y rueda mejoró la postura y perdió menos densidad sináptica, según Frontiers in Neurology. Podría acelerar la rehabilitación vestibular humana.

piezas.titulo: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.30016v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede una herramienta mapear todo el código y explicarlo? Code Comprehensor combina CodeGraph, un grafo de dependencias, CodeScribe, documentación jerárquica generada por modelo de lenguaje, y CodeContrast, un codificador dual texto‑código. En pruebas con OpenCV y un repositorio de cinco millones de líneas, CodeContrast supera noventa por ciento de fidelidad en la métrica RAGAS, lo que sugiere que podría acelerar la incorporación de nuevos desarrolladores y reducir el tiempo de refactorización.

piezas.titulo: Lifestyle Documentation in Therapy Evaluations for Autistic Children: A Lexicon-Based Analysis of Electronic Health Records.
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being. Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. Using electronic health records for children aged 2 to 18 diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (n = 5619 evaluation reports of n = 2021 unique patients), we classified health records based on the domains addressed.ResultsAcross notes, nutrition had the highest average degree of documentation ( M = 2.14), compared to activity ( M = 0.91), followed by wellness ( M = 0.66), and sleep ( M = 0.39). In occupational therapy, wellness was the most common (77.62% of notes), followed by physical activity (76.49% of notes), nutrition management (73.33% of notes), and sleep (34.97% of notes). The overall area under the curve (AUC) from the receiver operating characteristic analysis is 0.89.ConclusionsWhile it is encouraging that most evaluations addressed nutrition or physical activity, the near absence of attention to sleep represents a critical gap in care. Given sleep's foundational role in overall health and daily functioning, its omission is particularly concerning. Occupational therapists and interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams should more deliberately integrate WPH frameworks into their evaluations.

piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

destilado.texto: Los adultos con dislexia muestran recalibración fonética tanto con texto como con labios, aunque usan estrategias neuronales distintas. La resonancia funcional revela mayor activación bilateral del giro fusiforme en lectores disléxicos durante videos labiales, mientras lectores típicos activan más la zona frontal derecha con estímulos textuales. ¿Podría la diferencia cortical explicar la dificultad fonológica sutil?

piezas.titulo: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.30206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.

fuente.nota: Preprints sin revision por pares.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de capacidad: también de cómo se elige el experto durante la generación. MoEZip introduce una compresión del KV cache que considera la sensibilidad del enrutamiento, según métricas basadas en la información de Fisher. Con una retención del diez por ciento, el método supera al mejor precedente en varios benchmarks, lo que sugiere que la compresión agresiva puede mantenerse sin perder calidad.

piezas.titulo: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.30499v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.

destilado.texto: Construir un harness propio eleva ligeramente la eficiencia humana relativa en ARC-AGI-3, pero solo en dos revisiones. El estudio muestra que la mejora media es de unos tres puntos y que reducir el costo de inferencia puede empeorar el desempeño. ¿Podrá la IA superar a los humanos sin guía?

piezas.titulo: Agent Factory recap: Agent harnesses, shifting left, and autonomous coding
piezas.resumenOriginal: In this episode of The Agent Factory , we explore the reality of building with autonomous agents alongside Ryan Lopopolo, a software engineer at Google Cloud and the person who coined the term agent harness . From throwing out manual code editors to treating team collaboration like leveling up RPG stats, Ryan breaks down how grounding models in rich context and shifting interventions left unlocks high levels of agent autonomy. This post guides you through the key ideas from our conversation. Use it to quickly recap topics or dive deeper into specific segments with links and timestamps. The Agent Harness - What is it? Timestamp: [ 00:30 ] An AI agent as we're defining it here is a large language model (LLM) plus an agent harness . Think of the harness as everything wrapped around the LLM that isn't the model itself. For example, if you're working in Google Antigravity using Gemini 3.8 Flash , Gemini Flash is the LLM and Google Antigravity is the harness. While an unassisted model can answer simple questions out of the box, it can't check live conditions or interact with your workspace on its own. When a user asks a question like "Why is the sky blue?" , an unassisted LLM can respond without issue. However, when asked a question like "Should I wear a raincoat today?" , the model can't answer on its own because it lacks the necessary data. The harness catches the intent, queries live weather tools, bundles that context back into the prompt, and hands it to the model to produce an informed answer. Ryan Lopopolo on agent harnesses and autonomous coding Tilde Thurium sat down with Ryan Lopopolo to discuss what it takes to run fully autonomous coding workflows in production. See the summary below! Coining the harness and writing zero production code Timestamp: [ 02:22 ] The term agent harness grew out of Ryan's extensive work on autonomous coding agents, culminating in a February 2026 essay on leveraging coding models in an agent-first world. Ryan shared that he hasn't opened a traditional code editor since May of last year, maintaining that streak through his transition into Google Cloud . In this paradigm, engineers no longer author or review individual lines of syntax; instead, they operate at the level of natural language specifications and inspect the final artifacts, such as pull requests, documents, and spreadsheets. Then they determine whether the end result meets organizational standards. Harness engineering is the study and the practice of putting a model into an environment where it can succeed. If you don't do that work, you end up doing what I call 'prompt and pray'. Ryan Lopopolo Context curation and lazy prompting Timestamp: [ 03:35 ] Upfront harness investment pays off by allowing engineers to become lazy prompters. When the repository contains structured documentation, clear interfaces, and discoverable tools, you do not need to paste walls of text into a prompt box every morning "I aspire to be an incredibly lazy prompter. If I have done the job to give the model the tools and context it needs to ground itself, I don't need to write a long prompt. It figures it out." The model uses its harness to pull relevant context, allowing it to navigate large codebases and execute complex tasks without oversight. Shifting left: engineering best practices as autonomous guardrails Timestamp: [ 05:00 ] When an agent fails, developers face a whole spectrum of interventions. The most common reflex is to fiddle with the prompt or retry, but that never scales across a team. "The simplest, smooth-brain, stupidest intervention I can think of is literally just: try my prompt again without changing anything else. But shifting left means moving interventions earlier into the development lifecycle where they are cheapest and automated: from prompts, to repo docs, to linters, to tests, and all the way to upstream evals." Instead of hoping the model guesses right on the next turn, shifting left embeds standards directly into the environment. Linters, tests, and AGENTS.md files act as durable memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, making sure the agent stays on the rails without needing constant hand-holding. Leveraging established tools and determinism Timestamp: [ 06:50 ] Agents shine when they're handed tools that already mirror patterns heavily represented in pre-training data. Pairing models with standard command-line interfaces moves reasoning into determinism, shifting the burden of context aggregation away from the model and onto reliable tools. Ryan also shared an environmental design trick for context efficiency: structuring markdown files so link anchors sit directly beneath their corresponding prose blocks rather than inline. This prevents context clutter and mitigates "lost in the middle" retrieval issues. Because Ryan operates exclusively by reviewing end-state artifacts, keeping documentation readable allows him to easily inspect execution runs: "I want to be able to look at the pull request and review it. If it made a bad decision, I need to know where it went off the rails so I can whack the agent on the head and make sure it does not make that same mistake again." Long horizons and expanding the agentic loop Timestamp: [ 09:45 ] The central challenge of harness engineering is ensuring that agents cohere over long time horizons. Because human organizations produce software through iterative refinement rather than single-shot prompts, agent workflows must mirror that cadence. Harness engineering uses tightly scoped, reviewable pull requests to narrow the agent's state space. Stacking these high-confidence changes end-to-end allows supervisors to gradually expand the loop size, building trust until agents can autonomously execute large-scale initiatives, including entire language migrations Curating agent teams like RPG stats Timestamp: [ 11:58 ] Rather than divvying up sprint tasks based on individual specialties, having a diverse team contribute to an agent turns it into a central producer of work that carries everyone's strengths. Ryan compared leveling up an agent's capabilities to building out a character sheet: "[It's like] building out the stats of your RPG character. I get a new person on the team who is a React architect and boom! The attention that they pay is able to bump out the stats in front-end architecture and performance." With that collective expertise baked into the environment, the agent can autonomously classify incoming work and activate the exact skills it needs on demand, operating as both a backend architect and a front-end specialist. Accruing leverage in tools, not custom harnesses Timestamp: [ 14:38 ] For developers wondering whether to build their own custom agent harness, Ryan offered clear advice: don't build one from scratch. Standard harnesses already provide the foundational primitives: file reading, grep search, and command execution. Over-scaffolding an agent with rigid, bespoke frameworks creates technical debt and leads to sunk-cost traps when frontier models advance. "If you focus all of your efforts on improving quality on tools and context, you can freely adopt the newest models as they come out and you'll be constantly accruing leverage into a bit of the system that will never become obsolete." Operating Google Cloud and eliminating capability overhang Timestamp: [ 16:47 ] Discussing his work at Google Cloud , Ryan outlined his motivation to eliminate capability overhang : the delta between what frontier AI models are theoretically capable of and how much useful work is currently extracted in production. Because the cloud functions as a massive, programmable surface, equipping agents with direct interfaces to Google Cloud lets them manage and deploy infrastructure effectively, turning raw model capability into tangible enterprise utility. Continually updating your priors on AI Timestamp: [ 18:13 ] The speed of AI development requires engineers and teams to actively unlearn old limitations and constantly reassess what these models can achieve. " It's very important to continually be updating what you think is possible with these lovely tools that we have ," Ryan urged. What broke six months ago often runs effortlessly on today's frontier models. Rather than getting locked into rigid workflows, developers should build around the two highly extensible interfaces that will remain relevant across every model upgrade: tools and context. "Agents will always need context in order to do that last mile adaptation into what you think good is. And as you can continue to... shift it to the left, in terms of increasingly capable tools which act as a form of memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, you'll continually be amazed as the models are able to do more and more interesting things for you over time." How To Build A Custom Harness Next, Billy Jacobson started us off by showing how developers can customize their own agent harnesses for specific tasks. Under the hood: Why build a custom harness? Timestamp: [ 19:44 ] Before jumping into code, Billy unpacked why developers should understand the mechanics of a harness rather than treating it like a black box. Recalling advice from an engineering mentor that "You can just use the framework, but a great engineer will really understand the framework" , Billy explained that building a harness yourself is the best way to debug what happens when an agent breaks. You can evaluate three core design decisions for every workflow: Looping : How many iterations should the agent run, and what conditions trigger an exit state? Tools : What specific tools should the agent access, and when and how should it invoke them? Memory : How important is conversational and operational memory, and when should it be retrieved or compacted? Linear Agent Harness: Deterministic Single-Pass Execution Timestamp: [ 21:34 ] Billy demonstrated a minimalist linear harness designed for deterministic workflows where looping is unnecessary. This pattern is ideal for targeted inspections, file transformations, or single-turn data analyses where you want a high level of determinism and need the agent to perform the exact same execution flow every single time. Closed-Loop Agent Harness: Iterative Test-Driven Repair Timestamp: [ 22:45 ] When tasks demand active bug fixing and refactoring, a closed-loop harness provides the iterative reasoning required to reach a verified resolution. In this demo, Billy showcased an agent that applies an automated code edit to address a failing requirement, and the harness executes the unit test suite against the updated codebase. If the tests fail, the runtime captures standard failure logs and detailed stack traces, feeding those error diagnostics directly back into the agent's working memory. The process repeats continuously until all unit tests pass, backed by a five-iteration ceiling to prevent infinite loops and runaway execution costs. Guardrail Harness with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) Timestamp: [ 23:25 ] For developers who require custom behavior without rewriting core orchestration plumbing from scratch, Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) provides scaffolding with automated memory management and execution safeguards. Billy walked through an example that leverages ADK's native context compaction to summarize older conversational turns, preventing context window bloat during extended debugging runs. Custom interception hooks inspect and filter shell actions before execution, automatically stopping high-risk operations such as recursive file deletions, database drops, or unauthorized remote git pushes. This architecture gives teams fine-grained control over tool execution boundaries while avoiding the maintenance burden of bespoke harness frameworks. The 3-Layer Agent Dev Stack: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google Antigravity, and Google Skills Timestamp: [ 25:27 ] Next up, Smitha Kolan broke down why coding agents do not always require heavier reasoning models, emphasizing that high performance stems from balancing the three layers of the agent stack: Model , Harness , and Knowledge . "Your coding agent doesn't need a smarter model. It needs a better stack: model, harness, and knowledge. When all three click into place, everything changes." She then walked through the three tools she's been loving recently, one for each layer of the stack. Layer 1 | Model | Gemini 3.8 Flash : High-frequency agentic loops run between 20 and 60 sequential hops per task (inspecting files, updating functions, and executing unit tests). Because latency and API costs compound across iterations, a lightweight, responsive model like Gemini 3.8 Flash makes real-time agent loops practical without running up a massive bill. Layer 2 | Harness | Google Antigravity with /boost : Default Antigravity handles standard navigation and component creation. On top of that, the /boost command spins up an orchestrator that coordinates specialized sub-agents in parallel and concludes with an independent audit pass before modifying files. Layer 3 | Knowledge | Google Skills Repository : With over 19,000 GitHub stars and 100+ curated domain packages across Google Cloud, Firebase, Flutter, and Maps, this harness-agnostic repository injects precise domain context on demand, preventing agents from guessing cloud configurations Your turn to build Building effective coding agents requires moving past the reflex of simply swapping in larger models. As Ryan Lopopolo's philosophy of harness engineering illustrates, true developer leverage is achieved by shifting best practices to the left and investing in rich tools, deterministic verifiers, and well-curated context that survive model upgrades. When combined with fast inference models, structured orchestration harnesses, and modular domain knowledge, agents evolve from conversational novelties into dependable, autonomous engineering partners. Ready to put it into practice? Explore the tools and resources covered in this episode: Gemini 3.8 Flash : Fast, low-cost model for multi-hop agent loops. Google Antigravity ( /boost ): Orchestrator harness for parallel coding agents and verification. Google Skills : Modular domain knowledge for Google Cloud, Firebase, and Flutter. Agent Development Kit (ADK) : Custom harness middleware for safety guardrails and memory compaction. Full episode video : The full interview and live Factory Floor code demos. piezas.titulo: An organotypic hippocampo-prefrontal co-culture model for studying long-range connectivity and circuit plasticity
piezas.resumenOriginal: The hippocampal projection to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is a key component of brain networks involved in cognition and emotion. Here, we establish and validate an organotypic entorhino-hippocampo-prefrontal co-culture model that enables experimental investigation of long-range circuit connectivity and plasticity under controlled in vitro conditions. Anatomical tracing, viral labeling, and ultrastructural analyses demonstrate hippocampal axonal projections and synapse formation within the mPFC. Functional connectivity was supported by hippocampal CA1 stimulation, which evoked postsynaptic responses in 90.6% of recorded layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons. Intrinsic membrane properties and excitatory synaptic transmission were largely preserved across culture configurations. To demonstrate the experimental utility of the model, we examined the effects of selective alveus lesion and global activity blockade. Alveus lesion produced no detectable changes in the examined synaptic or intrinsic properties of mPFC neurons, whereas tetrodotoxin-mediated activity blockade increased miniature excitatory postsynaptic current frequency and reduced membrane capacitance. Together, these findings establish a versatile experimental platform for investigating long-range circuit connectivity and activity-dependent plasticity, with potential applications in mechanistic studies of neuromodulatory interventions.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Classroom-based observation and intervention of executive function for special education teachers working with preschoolers with Autism.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background/objectives Executive function (EF) related behavioral challenges are frequently observed in preschool children with autism spectrum disorder. However, structured, classroom-based observation of these behaviors by teachers remains difficult, resulting in limited practical assessment and recommendations for classroom-based support. This study aimed to examine the feasibility of teacher-administered EF assessment in special education centers and to formulate preliminary, expert-informed recommendations for autistic children with varying communication abilities. Methods A mixed-methods sequential design was used. A total of 793 children with autism aged 3-6 years were assessed by trained teachers. Multidisciplinary expert consultation was conducted to formulate preliminary recommendations for classroom activities based on age and communication profiles. Results Teachers achieved at least 85% accuracy in score conversion and interpretation, supporting the feasibility of its use in a special education classroom. Patterns of EF-related behavioral challenges observed in 793 children aged 3-6 years were integrated with existing evidence and multidisciplinary expert consensus to inform preliminary recommendations for classroom activities. Working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility were most evident, especially in children with limited verbal communication and those requiring intensive classroom support. Expert-informed classroom activities, including structured play, rule-changing games, memory-based exercises, emotional reflection tasks, and narrative planning, were subsequently suggested with increasing complexity across age groups and levels of communication ability. Conclusions The findings provide preliminary support for the teacher-administered MU.EF-102 of the classroom use and informed age- and communication-responsive, expert-informed classroom activity recommendations. The effectiveness of these recommendations requires evaluation in future intervention studies.

piezas.titulo: Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program
piezas.resumenOriginal: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “ Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges .” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments. The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations. To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks. One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance. The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall —has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms. No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program , developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society . Topics covered The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment. The topics are: Fundamental principles of design and functionality. Practical insights into advanced architectures. Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment. Emerging trends and evolving architectures. Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems. It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments. The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments. By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. AI-generated avatars explain concepts The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect. In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments. By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material. Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions. Modeling expert reasoning through dialogue The cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance. Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development. piezas.titulo: Preoperative cranial computed tomography in pediatric cochlear implantation: clinical necessity or optional step?
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectivesDue to growing evidence regarding the risks of ionizing radiation, especially in children, some centers now perform cochlear implantation (CI) without a preoperative computed tomography (CT) scan, relying solely on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study evaluates the necessity and safety of omitting CT scans before bilateral CI in children.MethodsA retrospective analysis of 164 children, implanted bilaterally between 2018 and 2024 and aged under 10 years at the time of either simultaneous or second CI, were included. The impact of preoperative imaging on duration of surgery and perioperative complications was analyzed. The surgical procedure was compared between cases with and without a preoperative CT scan and analyzed for surgeons in training and experienced surgeons.Results105 children were implanted with a preoperative CT scan and 59 without a CT scan. The duration of bilateral CI surgery was 122.5 (±41.4) min for procedures [CI without CT: 122.5 (±41.4) min; CI with CT: 116.1 (±33.84) min; (p = 0.4861)] and anesthesia [CI without CT: 237.2 (±47.38) min; CI with CT: 226.3 (±41.50) min; (p = 0.1352)] did not differ significantly between the groups, irrespective of the experience of the surgeons. Seven cases showed relevant malformations visible on MRI, such as large vestibular aqueduct syndrome, which were relevant during the surgery. Minor and major complications occurred rarely in both cohorts but more frequently in patients without CT scan (without CT: 10.2% (6/59); with CT: 4.8% (5/105); p = 0.2052; risk difference [RD], 5.4%; 95% CI, −6.3 to 14.3%). Intraoperative X-ray imaging revealed no cases of electrode tip fold-over, and no patients developed postoperative complete or incomplete facial nerve palsy.ConclusionIn summary, an MRI-based imaging strategy without routine preoperative CT may be safe and sufficient in appropriately selected pediatric CI candidates, with additional CT reserved for patients in whom clinical or MRI findings suggest relevant bony abnormalities, complex inner ear malformations, or syndromic conditions. This approach reduces unnecessary radiation exposure and the use of healthcare resources, while avoiding redundant diagnostic information from both imaging modalities, without compromising surgical safety or outcomes.

piezas.titulo: Prefrontal cortical morphometric covariance and cognitive task performance in healthy young adults: an exploratory analysis of Human Connectome Project data
piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

piezas.titulo: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
piezas.resumenOriginal: Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. piezas.titulo: Are clinician-administered ataxia scales truly culture-free? Rethinking contextual validity in diverse populations
piezas.resumenOriginal: Hereditary cerebellar ataxias are genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterized by substantial functional impairment. With the emergence of disease-modifying therapies and gene-targeted clinical trials, standardized and reliable clinical outcome measures are essential for assessing disease severity and progression. Among the available scales, two are widely used by clinicians to assess ataxia: The Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) and the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS). Given considerable linguistic, educational and sociocultural heterogeneity across the globe, we opine that it may pose challenges to the uniform application and cross-cultural comparability of these instruments. Published translations and adaptations were also examined to determine whether cultural adaptation extended beyond linguistic translation. Among all the identified adaptations, reported processes predominantly comprised forward and backward translation, expert review and assessment of linguistic, conceptual or cultural equivalence. These findings suggest that linguistic translation alone may not be sufficient to ensure that clinician-rated ataxia scales retain equivalent meaning and measurement across diverse populations. We therefore introduce the concept of “contextual validity” emphasizing that language, educational heterogeneity, literacy, graphomotor familiarity, cultural practices and testing environments that may influence performance independently of cerebellar dysfunction. This perspective outlines considerations for developing contextually adapted and psychometrically validated Indian-language versions of SARA and ICARS to improve measurement accuracy and support equitable clinical assessment and participation in global clinical trials.

piezas.titulo: From a surgeon's stroke to a third hemisphere—The auxilium architecture for brain restoration and extension
piezas.resumenOriginal: A surgeon was exercising on a stationary bicycle when he had a large ischemic left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, complicated by hemorrhagic transformation requiring hemicraniectomy and cranioplasty. He developed right-sided spastic hemiplegia and a mixed aphasia. This paper takes that case as its anchor to pose the question: beyond improving residual function, what would it mean to restore cognitive function that was lost so that the person fully returns to their pre-stroke baseline? Existing brain-computer interfaces rely on the person having an intact cortical substrate for intended movement and speech. Here we propose the Auxilium, a brain restoration architecture for the situation where that substrate is no longer present: an extracranial auxiliary brain system, agnostic to its substrate, that connects to a person's residual cortex through whatever input-output technology proves most appropriate, and that supplies, in parallel and in real time, new substrate, whether biological or synthetic. We address an assumption of brain-computer interface development, that throughput is the binding constraint. Linking a kHz brain to MHz digital does not impart the higher clock speed, because the limitation lies not in the port but in the architecture of the entire brain and body imparted by evolution. We posit that the substrate of canonical circuits and their integration areas is essential, and the Auxilium can be understood as restoring both connectivity (linkage between disconnected areas) and computation (information generation capability of a volume of neural tissue). We propose a near-term de-risking pipeline using stereoelectroencephalography during surgical epilepsy evaluation, comparing extracranial modules spanning threshold rules, PID controllers, expert systems, artificial neural networks, neuromorphic devices, and biological specimens, each linked in real time to a participant serving as their own control on naturalistic tasks. If ports alone restore the lost function, the requirement is routing connectivity. If performance improves only when the module supplies its own dynamics, the requirement is computational substrate. We expect the answer to depend on how much tissue was lost, how quickly, and on the individual's reserve, and we treat routing and substrate as endpoints of a continuum to be mapped empirically.

En cada iteración, se escriben 8 bytes, pero `dst` es una matriz de u32, por lo que cada elemento solo tiene espacio para 4 bytes. Eso significa que cada iteración sobrescribe parte del elemento anterior, lo que posiblemente lleve a una escritura fuera de los límites. Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2024-35809) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 17/05/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 15/10/2026 En el kernel de Linux, se ha resuelto la siguiente vulnerabilidad: PCI/PM: drena las devoluciones de llamada inactivas en tiempo de ejecución antes de eliminar el controlador. Una condición de ejecución entre la devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() y la devolución de llamada .remove() en el controlador PCI rtsx_pcr conduce a un crash de kernel debido a un error de página no controlado [1]. El problema es que no se espera que rtsx_pci_runtime_idle() se ejecute después de llamar a pm_runtime_get_sync(), pero esto último realmente no garantiza eso. Solo garantiza que las devoluciones de llamada de suspensión y reanudación no se ejecutarán cuando regrese. Sin embargo, si ya se está ejecutando una devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() cuando se llama a pm_runtime_get_sync(), este último notará que el estado de PM en tiempo de ejecución del dispositivo es RPM_ACTIVE y regresará de inmediato sin esperar a que se complete el primero. De hecho, no puede esperar a que se complete .runtime_idle() porque puede ser llamado desde esa devolución de llamada (podría decirse que no tiene mucho sentido hacerlo, pero no está estrictamente prohibido). Por lo tanto, en general, quien proporciona una devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() debe protegerla para que no se ejecute en paralelo con cualquier código que se ejecute después de pm_runtime_get_sync(). [Tenga en cuenta que .runtime_idle() no se iniciará después de que pm_runtime_get_sync() haya regresado, pero puede continuar ejecutándose si comenzó antes.] Una forma de abordar esa condición de ejecución es llamar a pm_runtime_barrier() después de pm_runtime_get_sync() (no antes porque es necesario un valor distinto de cero del contador de uso de PM en tiempo de ejecución para evitar que se invoquen devoluciones de llamada de PM en tiempo de ejecución) para esperar a que se complete la devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() en caso de que se esté ejecutando en ese punto. Un lugar adecuado para hacerlo es pci_device_remove() que llama a pm_runtime_get_sync() antes de eliminar el controlador, por lo que también puede llamar a pm_runtime_barrier() posteriormente, lo que evitará que se produzca la ejecución en cuestión, no sólo en el controlador rtsx_pcr, sino en cualquier controlador PCI que proporcione devoluciones de llamada .runtime_idle(). piezas.titulo: Intrinsic circadian organization of the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Introduction Circadian rhythms coordinate daily fluctuations in physiology and behavior, yet their organization within primary sensory pathways remains poorly defined. Although somatosensory responsiveness varies across the day-night cycle, it is unclear whether peripheral sensory circuits possess molecular mechanisms for temporal regulation. Objectives To determine whether the spinal-peripheral sensory axis harbors intrinsic circadian clocks and to define the molecular scope and functional organization of circadian regulation in dorsal root ganglia (DRGs). Methods We used real-time bioluminescence imaging to assess circadian oscillations of the core clock protein PER2 in the spinal dorsal horn and DRGs. To characterize molecular regulation, we performed RNA sequencing across a 52-hour circadian time course in DRGs. Results We demonstrate that the spinal dorsal horn and DRGs harbor robust, tissue-autonomous circadian clocks, with sustained PER2 oscillations. Circadian analysis identified 626 rhythmic genes (3.6% of expressed genes) in DRGs, with nonuniform phase distributions forming discrete temporal clusters. Functional annotation revealed phase-specific enrichment of processes including transport, neuronal structure, and proteostasis, suggesting coordinated temporal deployment of distinct molecular programs rather than uniform oscillations. Cross-referencing with neuropathic pain-associated genes revealed limited overlap; however, overlapping genes aligned to specific baseline phase windows enriched for regenerative annotations. Potassium channel-related signaling components implicated in neuropathic pain also showed baseline circadian modulation. Conclusion These findings establish the spinal dorsal horn and DRGs as intrinsically circadian tissues and reveal a temporally structured molecular landscape in DRG, providing a framework for understanding how peripheral sensory processing, plasticity, and homeostatic regulation are coordinated across the day-night cycle.

piezas.titulo: From virtual practice to real-world function the transfer problem in digital neurorehabilitation
piezas.resumenOriginal: Digital technologies have expanded opportunities for neurorehabilitation by enabling intensive, interactive, and adaptable motor practice. However, improvements achieved within virtual environments, rehabilitation games, or technology-based assessments do not necessarily translate into meaningful changes in everyday function. This Mini Review examines the transfer problem in digital neurorehabilitation and discusses key factors that may limit the generalization of training-related gains to real-world performance. We synthesize evidence regarding task specificity, sensory and perception-action differences between digital and physical environments, cognitive and contextual demands, practice variability, and patient-specific constraints that influence transfer. Based on these mechanisms, we propose a transfer-oriented framework consisting of five interconnected stages: skill acquisition, adaptive variability, cognitive-motor integration, contextualized real-world practice, and ecological evaluation. This framework emphasizes that transfer should be deliberately targeted rather than assumed as a consequence of successful digital training. We further discuss how virtual reality, augmented reality, wearable sensing, and hybrid rehabilitation models may support different stages of this process when integrated within adaptive and personalized approaches. Future digital rehabilitation research should move beyond evaluating performance within trained tasks and incorporate measures of functional and ecological transfer, including real-world mobility, activity, and participation. A shift from technology-centered rehabilitation toward transfer-oriented design may enhance the clinical impact of digital interventions and support meaningful improvements in daily life.

piezas.titulo: State-dependent responses of emotional brain networks in high myopia under blurred vision: a shift towards dorsal stream and cross-modal processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: PurposeReliable sensory input plays a vital role in shaping emotional experience, however, how the brain modulates the formation of emotion under chronic visual degradation remains unclear. Using high myopia (HM) as a natural model of sustained blur, this study investigated state-dependent responses of emotional brain networks during blurred movie viewing.MethodsTwenty-four participants with high myopia (HM) were tested without optical correction, comparing with normal vision (NV) controls from previous research. All participants watched thriller and scenic movie clips twice over one week during fMRI. Intra-subject synchrony and seed-based functional connectivity analyses focused on the amygdala and visual processing streams.ResultsCompared to NV controls, the HM group exhibited reduced intra-subject synchrony in visual cortices but increased synchrony in the primary auditory cortex, indicating cross-modal compensatory enhancement. During threat processing, HM participants showed strengthened and stable functional connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsal visual stream. For non-threatening content, this enhanced connectivity initially involved both dorsal and ventral stream but persisted selectively in the dorsal stream upon repeated viewing.ConclusionSustained visual blur elicits a perceptual-state-dependent functional response in emotional networks, characterized by heightened cross-modal auditory integration and an increased recruitment of the visual dorsal stream during blurred viewing. These findings highlight the brain’s immediate compensatory mechanisms under conditions of ambiguous visual input.

piezas.titulo: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.29139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

piezas.titulo: Building Presentation Intelligence for High-Quality Slide Generation
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.30888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: PowerPoint presentations (PPTs) are a dominant medium for communication across diverse domains, yet high-quality PPT generation still depends heavily on labor-intensive human effort. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for agentic tasks have created both new opportunities and challenges (Chen et al., 2026) for automatic PPT generation. In this work, we present a unified training framework for automatic PPT generation toward presentation intelligence, integrating cross-validated data synthesis, guided teacher enhancement, and verifiable reward optimization. We first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis, with explicit control over both difficulty and validity. We then develop a teacher-enhancement framework grounded in rules and prior knowledge to substantially strengthen the instructional capacity of teacher models. Building on this, we further improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through a mixed-teacher strategy and a lightweight outcome-driven trajectory filtering method. Finally, based on the resulting SFT models, we introduce a suite of verifiable aesthetic metrics together with a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to optimize slide-level visual attributes beyond text-only supervision. Experiments show that our enhanced SFT pipeline improves Qwen-3.6-27B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B by 7.45 and 9.35 points on PresentBench, respectively, surpassing GLM-5.2 while maintaining strong generalization. Reinforcement learning further improves performance across five aesthetic dimensions, compensating for the limitations of SFT in visual refinement. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for high-quality PPT generation.

piezas.titulo: Stroke Caregiver Education and Training in an Inpatient Sub-Acute Setting: A Retrospective Clinical Audit.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Caregiver burden is a significant issue post-stroke. Caregivers demonstrate unmet needs throughout the rehabilitation phase, with limited literature that delves into the details of caregiver education and training (CGET) provision prior to discharge. Objectives To identify current practice of multidisciplinary team documentation of CGET following stroke on an inpatient subacute neurosciences ward. Methods A retrospective clinical audit was conducted on 109 stroke admissions on an inpatient subacute neurosciences ward. Documented demographic information, admission and discharge Functional Independence Measure scores, and CGET from the multidisciplinary team were collected using a purpose-built audit tool. Descriptive analysis and sub-group comparison explored the findings against the Stroke Guideline recommendations. Results Data from 109 records were included, which identified 1398 episodes of CGET. Social work (SW) (79.9%) and occupational therapy (OT) (77.1%) documented CGET more consistently than other disciplines. CGET was significantly more likely to be documented for patients with cognitive impairment, yet only three of 28 (10.7%) individuals with memory impairment had documented CGET relating to memory strategies. Nursing staff documented minimal CGET across all domains, including management of continence. Conclusions Inconsistent CGET was documented for stroke recovery relating to activities of daily living, mobility and cognition. Variable documentation practices highlighted challenges with interpretation. Further research is needed to determine whether functional limitations of patients are being matched with the appropriate CGET. Practice implications multidisciplinary team caregiver education and training provision and documentation needs to be consistent, particularly relating to cognition, continence, mobility and activities of daily living.
